Keywords: Heriot Death Tax and Merchet Marriage Fine
Urban Liberty One Year and a Day
RagShortTexts: Serfs bound by corvée labor and marriage fines gained freedom by dwelling in chartered.

Variants.Content: Medieval serfs, called villeins in English custom, were bound to the soil and owed their lords a set of unfree dues. They had to work on the lord's demesne as corvée labor, and they paid customary fines: merchet on marriage, and heriot, the best beast of the household, on death. Yet the growth of chartered boroughs produced a legal principle that gave some serfs a way out. A serf who escaped to a town and lived there unclaimed for a year and a day could win permanent civic freedom, which was summed up in the maxim that city air makes a man free. Lords watched the towns closely, because each runaway was a loss of labor and dues.

As markets grew, lords began to commute labor services into money rents, and many accepted a manumission deed in return for cash. The coins let the lord buy arms, pay retainers, or fund a campaign, while the freed peasant kept his holding under a fixed rent. A lord who held out for old services risked losing tenants to the nearest borough.
Bailiff whips urge reapers through hot harvest days. Fleeing to a chartered town to apprentice in a cobbler's shop means surviving in hiding for twelve months to walk free forever.
